question: Define 'unlawful assembly' under Section 189 of the BNS. When does a lawful assembly become unlawful?
modelAnswer: Under s.189(1), an assembly of five or more persons is an unlawful assembly if the common object of its members is: (a) to overawe by criminal force, or show of criminal force, the Central Government, any State Government, Parliament, a State Legislature, or any public servant exercising his lawful powers; (b) to resist the execution of any law or legal process; (c) to commit mischief, criminal trespass or any other offence; (d) by criminal force or show of it, to take or obtain possession of property, deprive a person of a right of way, water or other incorporeal right, or enforce a right or supposed right; or (e) by criminal force or show of it, to compel a person to do what he is not legally bound to do or omit what he is legally entitled to do. The essentials are therefore the number (five or more), a shared common object, and that object being one of the five listed. Mere presence of five people is not enough — the object is decisive. The Explanation provides that an assembly lawful when it gathered may later become unlawful, for example when a peaceful meeting's members agree to use force. Under s.189(2), a person who, aware of the facts making the assembly unlawful, intentionally joins or continues in it is a member, punishable with up to six months, or fine, or both. The provision re-enacts s.141 IPC.

question: Explain the principle of constructive (vicarious) liability under Section 190 of the BNS. How does it differ from common intention under Section 3(5)?
modelAnswer: Section 190 (formerly s.149 IPC) provides that if a member of an unlawful assembly commits an offence in prosecution of the assembly's common object, or an offence the members knew was likely to be committed in prosecution of that object, every person who is a member at the time is guilty of that offence. It has two limbs: the first covers offences committed to achieve the common object itself; the second covers offences the members knew were likely to occur in pursuing it. An offence outside both limbs binds only the person who committed it. Section 190 does not create a separate offence; it makes members liable for the substantive offence, and the punishment and classification follow that offence. It differs from s.3(5) (common intention, formerly s.34 IPC) in several ways: s.190 needs at least five persons forming an unlawful assembly, s.3(5) needs only two or more; s.190 rests on a common object, which may arise on the spot without prior meeting of minds, while s.3(5) requires a common intention, a pre-arranged plan or meeting of minds; s.190 creates a specific liability through membership, while s.3(5) is a rule of evidence making each liable for acts done in furtherance of the common intention; and under s.3(5) participation in the criminal act is needed, whereas s.190 can attach through membership alone. BNSS s.359(3) allows a person liable under s.190 to compound an offence that is itself compoundable in like manner.

question: What is rioting under Section 191 of the BNS? What punishment does it carry, and what changed from the IPC?
modelAnswer: Under s.191(1), whenever force or violence is used by an unlawful assembly, or by any member of it, in prosecution of its common object, every member of the assembly is guilty of rioting. The ingredients are: an unlawful assembly of five or more persons; use of force or violence by the assembly or any member; that use being in prosecution of the common object; and the accused being a member. A member who personally used no force is still guilty, because the offence attaches to membership once force is used. Under s.191(2), rioting is punishable with imprisonment of either description up to two years, or fine, or both; it is cognizable, bailable and triable by any Magistrate. Under s.191(3), rioting while armed with a deadly weapon, or anything which used as a weapon is likely to cause death, is punishable with up to five years, or fine, or both, triable by a Magistrate of the first class. The BNS merges ss.146-148 IPC into one section and raises the maximum for armed rioting from three years (s.148 IPC) to five years.

question: Distinguish between rioting (Section 191) and affray (Section 194).
modelAnswer: Rioting and affray both disturb public peace but differ in their ingredients. (1) Number: rioting requires an unlawful assembly of five or more persons; affray requires only two or more. (2) Common object: rioting requires force or violence used in prosecution of a common object in s.189(1); affray needs no common object — only fighting. (3) Place: rioting may take place anywhere, including private premises; affray must occur in a public place. (4) Disturbance: affray must disturb the public peace; rioting needs no proof of actual disturbance of the peace beyond use of force or violence. (5) Liability: in rioting every member of the assembly is guilty even if he personally did not use force; in affray only those who actually fight are liable. (6) Punishment: rioting is punishable with up to two years (five years if armed); affray with up to one month, or fine up to ₹1,000, or both. Both are cognizable and bailable and triable by any Magistrate (except armed rioting, triable by a Magistrate of the first class). The BNS raised the affray fine from ₹100 under s.160 IPC to ₹1,000.

question: List the offences created by sub-sections (2) to (9) of Section 189, with their punishments.
modelAnswer: Section 189 consolidates several IPC provisions. (2) Being a member of an unlawful assembly — knowingly joining or continuing in it: up to six months, or fine, or both (s.143 IPC). (3) Joining or continuing in an unlawful assembly knowing it has been lawfully commanded to disperse: up to two years, or fine, or both (s.145 IPC). (4) Being a member while armed with a deadly weapon or a thing likely to cause death: up to two years, or fine, or both (s.144 IPC). (5) Knowingly joining or continuing in any assembly of five or more persons likely to disturb the public peace after it has been lawfully commanded to disperse: up to six months, or fine, or both; if the assembly is actually unlawful, sub-s. (3) applies (s.151 IPC). (6) Hiring, engaging, employing, promoting or conniving at the hiring of persons to join an unlawful assembly: punishable as a member and for any offence the hired person commits as a member (s.150 IPC). (7) Harbouring, receiving or assembling hired persons in premises one controls: up to six months, or fine, or both (s.157 IPC). (8) Being engaged or hired, or offering to be hired, to do any act in sub-s. (1): up to six months, or fine, or both; and (9) going armed or offering to go armed when so hired: up to two years, or fine, or both (s.158 IPC). All are cognizable and bailable and triable by any Magistrate, except that for sub-s. (6) bailability and trial follow the offence.

question: Explain Section 196 of the BNS on promoting enmity between different groups. How does it differ from Section 153A IPC?
modelAnswer: Section 196(1) punishes three kinds of conduct. Clause (a): by words spoken or written, signs, visible representations, electronic communication or otherwise, promoting or attempting to promote disharmony or feelings of enmity, hatred or ill-will between different religious, racial, language or regional groups, castes or communities, on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, caste or community or any other ground. Clause (b): committing an act prejudicial to the maintenance of harmony between such groups which disturbs or is likely to disturb the public tranquillity. Clause (c): organising or participating in an exercise, movement or drill meant for, or likely to result in, participants using or being trained to use criminal force or violence against such a group, where it causes or is likely to cause fear, alarm or a feeling of insecurity among its members. The punishment is up to three years, or fine, or both. Under s.196(2), if the offence is committed in a place of worship or an assembly engaged in religious worship or ceremonies, it is punishable with up to five years and fine. Both are cognizable, non-bailable and triable by a Magistrate of the first class. Compared with s.153A IPC, the substance and punishments are unchanged; the main textual change is the express mention of 'electronic communication', bringing social-media and online content clearly within the offence.

question: Discuss Section 197 of the BNS. What new offence does clause (d) create?
modelAnswer: Section 197 (formerly s.153B IPC) protects national integration. By words, signs, visible representations, electronic communication or otherwise, it punishes: (a) making or publishing an imputation that a class of persons, because they belong to a religious, racial, language or regional group, caste or community, cannot bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution or uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India; (b) asserting, counselling, advising, propagating or publishing that such a class shall be denied or deprived of their rights as citizens; (c) making or publishing an assertion, counsel, plea or appeal about the obligation of such a class that causes or is likely to cause disharmony or enmity, hatred or ill-will between its members and others; and (d) making or publishing false or misleading information jeopardising the sovereignty, unity and integrity or security of India. Clause (d) is new: it targets the spreading of false or misleading information, including fake news, where it endangers India's sovereignty, unity, integrity or security, even if no particular group is targeted. The punishment is up to three years, or fine, or both, and up to five years plus fine if committed in a place of worship or religious assembly. The offence is cognizable, non-bailable and triable by a Magistrate of the first class.

question: What does Section 195 of the BNS provide? How has it changed from Section 152 IPC?
modelAnswer: Section 195 protects public servants who are dispersing an unlawful assembly or suppressing a riot or affray. Under s.195(1), whoever assaults or obstructs such a public servant, or uses criminal force on him, in the discharge of that duty, is punishable with imprisonment of either description up to three years, or with fine which shall not be less than ₹25,000, or with both. This is cognizable, bailable and triable by a Magistrate of the first class. Under s.195(2), whoever threatens to assault, attempts to obstruct, or threatens or attempts to use criminal force on such a public servant is punishable with up to one year, or fine, or both; this is non-cognizable, bailable and triable by any Magistrate. Section 152 IPC covered actual assault and obstruction and mere threats or attempts together, with the same punishment of three years, or fine, or both. The BNS separates the two: actual assault or obstruction keeps the three-year maximum and adds a minimum fine of ₹25,000 where fine is imposed, while threats and attempts get a lower maximum of one year.

question: Explain the liability of the owner or occupier of land under Section 193 of the BNS.
modelAnswer: Section 193 makes persons connected with land liable for failing to help keep the peace on it. Under s.193(1), when an unlawful assembly or riot takes place, the owner or occupier of the land where it happens, and any person having or claiming an interest in the land, is punishable with fine up to ₹1,000 if he or his agent or manager, knowing that the offence is being or has been committed, or having reason to believe it is likely, fails to give the earliest possible notice to the officer in charge of the nearest police station, and fails to use all lawful means to prevent it and, once it takes place, to disperse or suppress it. Under s.193(2), when a riot is committed for the benefit or on behalf of a person who owns, occupies or claims an interest in the land concerned, or in the subject of the dispute, or who has accepted or derived any benefit from it, that person is punishable with fine if he or his agent or manager, having reason to believe the riot or assembly was likely, did not use all lawful means to prevent and suppress it. Under s.193(3), the agent or manager of such a person is separately punishable with fine on the same basis. All three are non-cognizable, bailable and triable by any Magistrate. The section merges ss.154-156 IPC.

question: Problem: Ten members of a village faction gather armed with lathis to forcibly harvest a crop on land in dispute with a rival. When the rival's family resists, one member, K, pulls out a hidden knife and stabs a rival, killing him. The others had not known K had a knife. Discuss the liability of the members.
modelAnswer: First, the gathering is an unlawful assembly under s.189(1)(d): ten persons with the common object of taking possession of property, and enforcing a claimed right, by criminal force or show of criminal force. Every person who knowingly joined it is a member under s.189(2), and those carrying lathis may be liable under s.189(4) if the lathis are things likely to cause death when used as weapons. Second, force was used in prosecution of the common object when they met the rival's resistance, so every member is guilty of rioting under s.191(1); the members armed with lathis face armed rioting under s.191(3) (up to five years). Third, liability for the death depends on s.190. K is directly liable for murder. For the others, the question is whether causing death was committed in prosecution of the common object, or was known to be likely. Their object was to harvest the crop by force; it did not include killing. But an armed faction setting out to take a disputed crop by force, carrying lathis, may well have known that serious injury or death was a likely consequence of resistance. On the other hand, the others did not know K had a knife, which suggests a knife killing was beyond what they contemplated. A court would likely hold the other members liable under s.190 for an offence they knew was likely — possibly culpable homicide or grievous hurt, depending on the facts — but not necessarily for murder, which may fall outside the second limb. K alone would then be liable for murder under s.103. The answer turns on the evidence of what the members knew was likely.

question: What is the offence under Section 192 of the BNS (provocation to riot)?
modelAnswer: Section 192 (formerly s.153 IPC) punishes a person who, malignantly, or wantonly by doing anything illegal, gives provocation to any person intending, or knowing it to be likely, that the provocation will cause rioting. The provoker need not be a member of the assembly or take part in the riot; the offence lies in the provocation itself. The punishment depends on the result: if rioting is committed as a consequence of the provocation, up to one year, or fine, or both; if rioting is not committed, up to six months, or fine, or both. The offence is cognizable, bailable and triable by any Magistrate. The two key mental elements are the malignant or wanton character of the act and the intention or knowledge that rioting is likely.
